newsitem.title: USA: Viacom chief viewed as tough, tenacious.
newsitem.headline: Viacom chief viewed as tough, tenacious.

text.p: Viacom Inc Chairman, President and Chief Executive Sumner Redstone is known as an aggressive, tenacious manager who isn't afraid to put on a good fight.
Whether it's clinging to the side of a burning building while flames engulfed his body or arguing his case in court, Redstone is viewed as a tough competitor who won't back down.
"He's known for endurance," Josephthal Lyon & Ross analyst Dennis McAlpine said. "He'll take anybody on."
Redstone, a 73-year-old Harvard educated lawyer whose father managed a small group of drive-in movie theaters, may have one of his toughest battles ahead: rebuilding confidence among investors.
Viacom, which was acquired by Redstone in 1987, saw its stock hit a 52-week low on Tuesday, tumbling 3-3/4 to 27-1/4 in afternoon trading. By mid-afternoon, close to 5 million shares had been traded.

The stock dropped after the company said Blockbuster Chairman and Chief Executive Bill Fields had decided to resign, and that the unit's operating cash flow was expected to be down between 15 percent and 20 percent in the first quarter.
Fields' departure comes about a year after Viacom Chief Executive Frank Biondi was ousted. Fields had joined Blockbuster in March 1996, arriving at the company from Wal-Mart Stores Inc.

At the time of Biondi's departure, several news reports cited unnamed sources saying that Redstone was disappointed with the company's performance and decided to take back the reigns. Redstone assumed Biondi's title and his duties.
On the day Biondi left, the company's stock closed at 40-5/8. It has slid further since as the company continues to try to turn around its Blockbuster unit.

"It's a weird situtation in that they made a very strong presentation in October," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said. "And then, in a matter of four to five months, the situation went from bad to worse."
"It's unsettling, particularly when someone's only been there a year," and since Blockbuster is viewed as a "swing factor" in Viacom's overall health, he added.

Several analysts said they did not believe Fields was being forced out by Redstone. However, they said they found it troubling that Fields would leave so soon after arriving, and were worried that his successor will need at least a year to get up to speed.
It remains to be seen whether Redstone's aggressive posture at Viacom is what the company needs.
However, analysts are quick to note that it was Redstone who turned Viacom into a giant entertainment company that is involved in movie making, cable television, book publishing and video retailing.
Redstone, who served in the Truman administration as a lawyer in the Justice Department, joined his father's privately held company, National Amusements Inc, in 1954.
He was named president and chief executive of National Amusements in 1967.
His legal background was well-used at National Amusement since theater owners are frequently at odds with movie studios.
"Redstone is known for certain litigiousness," McAlpine said. "He'll sue somebody at the drop of a hat, and he usually wins."

That toughness was perhaps never more evident than when, in 1979, he climbed out of a hotel window to escape a fire in Boston. He clung to the ledge, not letting go for at least 10 minutes until he could be rescued.
It's tidbits like that that led one analyst to say of Redstone: "I wouldn't count him out."
